Philip the Apostle
FIL-ip thuh uh-POS-uhl
proper noun
One of the twelve apostles, of Bethsaida; Greek Philippos, “lover of horses”; to be distinguished from Philip the evangelist of Acts.

Biblical Definition

Philip the apostle was one of the Twelve, a man of Bethsaida in Galilee, the same town as Peter and Andrew, and he is to be distinguished from Philip the evangelist and deacon of the book of Acts. The Gospel of John gives us our clearest glimpses of him. Called by the Lord with the simple word Follow me, Philip at once sought his friend Nathanael: We have found him, of whom Moses in the law and the prophets did write, Jesus of Nazareth—and when Nathanael doubted, Philip answered with the best of all invitations, Come and see. It was to Philip the Lord tested the question of feeding the five thousand; and when certain Greeks came up to the feast desiring to see Jesus, they came to Philip. In the upper room Philip made the request that drew out one of the Lord’s greatest sayings: Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us—to which Jesus answered, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. The dictionary reads Philip the apostle as the disciple who found the Lord and at once brought another, and whose honest, half-understanding question opened to the church the truth that to see Christ is to see the Father—a reminder that the apostles were plain men brought along slowly into great light, and that the answer to every seeker remains, Come and see.

Webster 1828 Definition

One of the Twelve, of Bethsaida; who brought Nathanael with “Come and see,” and whose request “shew us the Father” drew out the Lord’s word that to see Him is to see the Father.

PHILIP THE APOSTLE, one of the Twelve, of Bethsaida in Galilee.

To be distinguished from Philip the evangelist of Acts.

Brought Nathanael to Christ with “Come and see” (Joh 1:45).

The Greeks who would see Jesus came to Philip (Joh 12:21).

“Shew us the Father” drew out the Lord’s great answer (Joh 14:8–9).

Key Scripture

Joh 1:45 — "Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."

Joh 14:8 — "Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us."

Joh 14:9 — "Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?"

Joh 12:21 — "The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though Philip the apostle is often confused with Philip the evangelist; the chief truth is his witness that to see Christ is to see the Father.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to clarify is the common confusion of the two Philips of the New Testament. Philip the apostle was one of the Twelve, called early in John’s Gospel; Philip the evangelist was one of the seven chosen to serve tables in Acts 6, who later preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch. They are two men, and the careful reader keeps them distinct. Beyond this, no great corruption attends the apostle; the chief thing is rather to receive the truth his questions drew out and not to pass him by as a minor figure.

The principle to recover is the great truth Philip’s request occasioned: that to see Christ is to see the Father. When Philip said, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us, the Lord answered, He that hath seen me hath seen the Father—for the Son is the express image of the Father’s person, and in Him the invisible God is made known. Philip’s honest, half-understanding request opened to the church one of the clearest words of Christ’s deity and His revelation of the Father. And his first act after being found—to find Nathanael and say, Come and see—remains the model of the disciple who, having found the Lord, brings another to Him.
